text: Science is frequently described. <break time="0.8s" /> As the principles informing an activity. <break time="0.8s" /> A method that starts with a question. <break time="0.8s" /> Phrased as a statement, or a hypothesis. <break time="0.8s" /> Which progresses to being tested against observations. <break time="0.8s" /> In a contrived, experimental environment. <break time="0.8s" /> And eventually ends in a definitive conclusion. <break time="0.8s" /> But history commonly recognises people as scientists. <break time="0.8s" /> And even praises them. <break time="0.8s" /> For their contributions to scientific knowledge. <break time="0.8s" /> Who have not strictly followed such a method. <break time="0.8s" /> Physics is full of amazing discoveries. <break time="0.8s" /> That have resulted not so much from experimentation. <break time="0.8s" /> But from mathematical deductions. <break time="0.8s" /> Or even numerous hours of patiently watching the sky. <break time="0.8s" /> Or perhaps looking through photographs. <break time="0.8s" /> The discovery of phenomena such as black holes or subatomic particles. <break time="0.8s" /> Is often seeded in extrapolations that we typically think of as scientific. <break time="0.8s" /> Long before they are found or identified. <break time="0.8s" /> By an experiment under controlled conditions. <break time="0.8s" /> While evolution can be demonstrated in the laboratory today. <break time="0.8s" /> Darwin had no such luxury. <break time="0.8s" /> And relied on comparisons he could make between diverse environments.
